activities.anchor: Industry surveys (Anaconda's State of Data Science
activities.caption: call the preparation tax
activities.name: dePrepEst

config.prompt: Industry surveys put roughly what share of a data scientist's working time on data preparation — loading and cleaning — before any modelling?
config.why: Around 40–45% — industrialising that preparation once, in tested pipelines, buys back nearly half an organisation's analytical capacity.
config.context: one that leaves it to individuals repeats the same cleaning work in every notebook

activities.anchor: tables whose semantics (what a row means)
activities.caption: pair each deliverable property with its question
activities.name: deDeliverMatch

config.prompt: The engineering layer's deliverable is tables with explicit properties — pair each with the question it answers:

pairs.right: how far behind reality they run

config.why: So a data scientist asking 'is this number right?' gets an answer from a document and a test suite instead of an afternoon of archaeology.

activities.caption: ETL or ELT — file each claim
activities.name: deEltSort

config.prompt: File each claim under the load order it describes:

items.label: transform before storing, because warehouses were expensive
load raw first, in its original messy form
transform inside the warehouse with SQL
the transform destroyed the original — March bugs unrecoverable

config.why: Cloud warehouses inverted the economics: keeping raw data permanently makes every transform re-runnable from source, so history can be rebuilt correctly.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the layered architecture
activities.name: deLayerCloze

config.text: The layered architecture: a %%0%% layer exactly as landed, a %%1%% layer that deduplicates and types each source, and %%2%% layer models shaped for specific business questions. Each layer is rebuilt from the one below, and only the bottom layer is allowed to surprise you.
config.hint: Three metals' worth of medallions, bottom to top.

activities.caption: rebuild the nightly dependency chain
activities.name: deChainOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the nightly chain — what comes first:
config.why: Pipelines are graphs of dependencies, not scripts — the scheduler walks the DAG, retrying failed nodes with backoff and backfilling missed runs after an outage.

activities.anchor: data pipelines are just scheduled SQL
activities.caption: find the backwards claim — the hard 80%
activities.name: deSqlSpot

config.prompt: One of these pipeline claims is backwards — click it:
lines: The SQL is the easy 20% of the work.
Idempotent tasks are safe to re-run twice — because they will run twice.
Late-arriving data and timezone drift are exactly the failure modes an orchestrator manages.
Teams that budget only for the SQL ship the other 80% as features.
config.correction: Teams that budget only for the SQL ship the other 80% as incidents.
config.why: The hard 80% is everything around the SQL: idempotency, late data, schema evolution, credential rotation, and who is accountable when a number is wrong.

activities.caption: true or false — the celebrated drop
activities.name: deStatusJudge

config.statement: A payment provider's dashboards suddenly report a 40% drop in failures. Without data tests, the right response is to celebrate the improvement.
config.why: The provider changed a status code from "FAILED" to "failed_declined" — a distribution test on the status column catches it within the hour, and the fix is a mapping table rather than a retraction.

activities.anchor: Every pipeline has a latency budget
activities.caption: batch versus streaming — drag the divider
activities.name: deClockCompare

config.prompt: Two clocks for the same events — drag the divider:

before.label: batch
before.text: hourly or daily jobs — simple, cheap, replayable; each run sees a fixed slice of history

after.label: streaming
after.text: events processed within seconds — with watermarks for out-of-order arrivals and roughly 5–10× the engineering complexity

config.why: The expert default is batch until a measured business decision requires faster — streaming's value decays within minutes only for fraud scoring, live dashboards and alerting.

config.prompt: 100 analysts each run 20 unpartitioned full-table scans a day over a 1-terabyte fact table, at roughly $6 per terabyte scanned. Roughly what does the habit burn per day?
config.why: 100 × 20 × 1 TB × $6 ≈ $12,000 a day — for answers a partition prune would deliver for about $33. Partitioning and pruning decide the warehouse bill.
config.context: a query filtered to one day scans 1/365th of the table and costs 1/365th of the money

activities.anchor: Schema evolution is the quiet test
activities.caption: the 'temporary' rename
activities.name: deSchemaBranch

config.root: An upstream team renames a column 'temporarily'. What does a mature platform do?

choices.label: Registry-checked contracts reject the breaking producer at deploy time
choices.feedback: Producers declare the schema they write; compatibility rules reject breaking changes at deploy, not at 3 a.m. in a dashboard.

choices.label: Downstream readers adapt whenever they notice
choices.feedback: That is the failure: downstream silently mis-reports for weeks — what breaks is not the pipeline but everyone's trust in the numbers.

choices.label: Nothing — a column name is cosmetic
choices.feedback: Tables outlive the applications that write them; the rename breaks every downstream reader that survives on yesterday's shape.

contract.text: Additive-by-default migrations and versioned tables let a consumer pin itself to last year's shape.

trust.text: 'Move fast and break things' fails quietly here — and the thing broken is trust.

config.why: Explicit contracts, additive migrations and versioned tables are the mature patterns; the data contract imports software engineering's API discipline into data.
